newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower, range-trading foreseen.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower, range-trading foreseen.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Monday, following a lackluster London session, with many participants sidelined until Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's mid-week Congressional testimony.
The Fed Chairman delivers the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony on February 26-27.
In early dealings, the 30-year Treasury bond was down 5/32 to 99-21/32, yielding 6.65 percent. Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-1/32, yielding 5.85 percent.
U.S. Treasury volume was light overseas before the Fed Chairman's testimony on Wednesday and Thursday, traders said.
Analysts said the market was likely to trade in narrow ranges, at least until Greenspan completes his testimony.

No major economic data are due before the testimony. The government will report January Federal budget figures at 1400 EST/1800 GMT on Monday, data that should not move the market. Weekly chain and department store sales surveys are due on Tuesday, as are data on January import and export prices and the Conference Board's consumer confidence index.

"Investors will freeze in place or slink towards cash today and tomorrow (before Greenspan gives) his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins readings to Congressional committees on Wednesday and Thursday," said David Munro, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics.

Bill Hornbarger, fixed-income strategist at A.G. Edwards & Sons, said the market has established a "nicely defined range" for the 30-year Treasury bond yield between 6.50 percent and 6.85 or 6.90 percent.
"People are pretty comfortable with that," he said.

Munro said Greenspan will be "hawkish in word, just to minimize the need to be hawkish in deed later." The Fed Chairman could apply that hawkish tone both to the stock market which has risen 10 percent since his "irrational exuberance" remark and to "the slowly rising heat in wage gains," Munro said.
"People are a little fearful of what Greenspan might say in the Humphrey-Hawkins testimony," said Josh Feinman, vice president and global markets economist at Bankers Trust.
"Greenspan will say things look good, but he'll probably reemphasize that there are risks," said Feinman.
Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets, said Greenspan's testimony would not sound terribly hawkish.

"He's going to sound pretty sanguine about the current state of the economy and its near-term prospects," he said. "Clearly, things are going his way. We're looking at an economy that had considerable forward momentum and in which inflation in surprisingly well behaved. There's not much to warn about other than the boilerplate language that the Fed should remain vigilant about inflation."
The market faces some fresh supply this week.

In addition to its weekly bill auction on Monday -- $26.0 billion in 3- and 6-month bills, the Treasury will sell $17.5 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
Though bids for the two-year notes are due on Tuesday afternoon, a day before the Greenspan testimony, analysts said the market should have little trouble absorbing new supply.
Trading on a when-issued basis, the two-year notes to be sold on Tuesday were yielding 5.8775 percent and the five-year notes to be sold on Wednesday were yielding 6.1825 percent.
In early dealings, three-, six-, and year-bill rates were each up two basis points to 4.98 percent, 5.04 percent and 5.20 percent, respectively.
Ten-year notes were down 6/32 to 98-30/32, yielding 6.40 percent.
